warmup.q: The payment program describes its records in a schema, a list of numbered fields that the writer and every reader keep a copy of, like the café's blank form. Version 1 has int64 amount_minor = 3: field 3 is the amount, a whole number. Version 2 deletes that field. A year later, version 3 adds int64 fee_minor = 3, the shop's fee, and gives it number 3 because the number was free. A program still on version 1 reads a version 3 payment whose fee is 150. What does it see?
options: An error, because the field names don't match
An amount of 150, with no error
An amount of 0, because the field was deleted
A field number it doesn't know, which it skips
warmup.why: Names never travel in the bytes, only numbers. The bytes say "field 3, a whole number, 150". Version 1's schema says field 3 is amount_minor, so the old program reads 150 as the amount. Same number, same type, new meaning, and nothing notices. It's the café reprinting box 3 with a new question while old blanks still hang on kitchen walls. The last option is what happens with a number the reader has never seen, which is why the second section reserves deleted numbers for good.

sections.h: Put a number on each field: how Protobuf writes a record
sections.html:
From objects to bytes followed one card payment: a Kotlin object holding a payment number, the shop's name, an amount, a currency and two tags. It ended with the payment written as a bare list of its five values. That took 39 bytes, against 84 with the field names. (A byte is a number from 0 to 255, made of eight bits, ones and zeros.) But a bare list works only if the writer and the reader agreed beforehand what the first, second and third values are. Write that agreement down, give a copy to both sides, and you have a schema: a description of a record's fields and their types, kept apart from the data. In the café, the schema is the blank form on the kitchen wall.

Protocol Buffers, or Protobuf, is the most common way to do this in Java and Kotlin programs. It's a binary format, one that writes numbers as raw bytes rather than as readable text. Google built it for its own programs and published it in 2008. You describe the record in a .proto file, a short text file that both sides share:

syntax = "proto3";

message Authorization {
  int64  payment_id   = 1;
  string merchant     = 2;
  int64  amount_minor = 3;   // 4000 means 40.00
  string currency     = 4;
  repeated string tags = 5;
}

message starts the description of one kind of record. Each line inside it names a field, its type and a number. int64 is a 64-bit whole number, string is text, and repeated means a list. The = 1 and = 2 aren't default values. They're field numbers, the numbered boxes of the form, and they go into the bytes in place of the names.

Encoding turns a record into bytes, and decoding turns the bytes back. In Protobuf's bytes, each field becomes a key followed by a value. The key packs two things into one number: the field number times 8, plus a wire type from 0 to 7. (That puts the wire type in the key's lowest three bits.) The wire type tells a reader how to find the end of the value, even for a field it doesn't know. Two wire types cover most records. Type 0 is a varint, for whole numbers. Type 2, called LEN, is a length followed by that many bytes, for text, raw bytes and lists. (Types 1 and 5 are numbers of a fixed 8 and 4 bytes.)

A varint stores a whole number in as few bytes as it needs. Each byte holds 7 bits of the number, lowest bits first, and its top bit, the eighth, says whether another byte follows. Take 4000, which is 1111 1010 0000 in binary. The lowest seven bits, 010 0000, go first with the top bit set, which gives a0 in hexadecimal (base 16, where each byte is written as two digits from 00 to ff). The bits that are left, 1 1111 (31), go next with the top bit clear: 1f. So 4000 is a0 1f. Every number below 128 takes one byte.

Here is the whole payment as it travels between programs, or "on the wire", as programmers say of bytes crossing a network:

08 91 80 ed 83 b4 b4 ec d4 19    field 1, varint: 1849204436731904017
12 0b 46 65 72 6e 20 42 61 ...   field 2, length 11: "Fern Bakery"
18 a0 1f                         field 3, varint: 4000
22 03 45 55 52                   field 4, length 3: "EUR"
2a 04 63 61 72 64                field 5, length 4: "card"
2a 03 33 64 73                   field 5 again: "3ds"

That's 42 bytes, against 84 for MessagePack (a binary form of JSON that keeps the names) and 116 for JSON text. Field 1's key is 1 times 8 plus 0, which is 08. Field 2's is 2 times 8 plus 2, which is 18, or 12 in hex. A list field repeats the same key once per item. The stepper below decodes the bytes one key at a time.

Varints are cheap for small numbers and costly for large or negative ones. The 64-bit payment number takes 9 bytes as a varint; declared as fixed64, a type that always uses 8 bytes, it would take a flat 8. Negative numbers are worse. A computer stores -1 in a 64-bit field with all 64 bits set (a scheme called two's complement), so a plain int64 needs 10 bytes for it. For fields that are often negative, sint64 first applies ZigZag, which turns 0 into 0, -1 into 1, 1 into 2, -2 into 3 and so on. Then -1 takes one byte. The type you declare decides the bytes, so pick it for the values you expect.

The bytes carry numbers, wire types and values, and no names at all. Next, we'll change the schema and see whether old code can still read them.

try.title: Walk the bytes with protobuf-java
steps: Open ProtoBytesDemo.kt. It builds the payment's schema in code (the same thing protoc, Protobuf's compiler, makes from the .proto file), encodes the record, and walks the bytes one key at a time with CodedInputStream, protobuf-java's byte reader.
Predict before you run it: how many bytes does the payment number take as int64, and as fixed64? How many does -1 take as int64, and as sint64?
Run it from the labs folder with the command below.

code.title: ProtoBytesDemo.kt (the walking part)
code.html: val input = CodedInputStream.newInstance(bytes) while (!input.isAtEnd) { val start = input.totalBytesRead val key = input.readTag() val field = WireFormat.getTagFieldNumber(key) // key ushr 3 val type = WireFormat.getTagWireType(key) // key and 7 val value = when (type) { WireFormat.WIRETYPE_VARINT -> input.readInt64().toString() WireFormat.WIRETYPE_LENGTH_DELIMITED -> "\"" + input.readStringRequireUtf8() + "\"" else -> { input.skipField(key); "(skipped)" } } val raw = bytes.copyOfRange(start, input.totalBytesRead) println("key %02x = field %d, wire type %d %-24s %s".format(key, field, type, value, hex(raw))) }

video.title: Numbers instead of names: how Protobuf writes a payment in 42 bytes

sections.h: Old code skips what it doesn't know: unknown fields and the rules for change
sections.html:
Now the schema changes. The team that looks for fraud adds a risk score, a number from 0 to 100 that says how suspicious a payment looks:

  int64 risk_score = 6;

Programs are updated one at a time, never all at once. To deploy a program is to install its new version and start it. The payment program is deployed first, and starts writing field 6. The program that pays the shops each night still runs last month's version, which has never heard of field 6. Its reader meets the key 0x30, which is 48, or 6 times 8 plus 0: field 6, a varint. It reads one varint, and then it has nowhere to put the value. So it keeps the bytes aside as an unknown field, the way the night cook staples box 6 to the back of the order and passes it on. Without the wire type, it couldn't even tell where field 6 ends.

Old code reading data written by new code is called forward compatibility. The other direction is backward compatibility: new code reading old data. A payment written before the change has no field 6, so the new code gets the default value, 0.

Keeping unknown fields matters more than it looks. Say the payout program reads a payment, changes its amount and writes it back. protobuf-java, Protobuf's library for Java and Kotlin, writes field 6 back out too, so the risk score survives. That wasn't always so. Proto3, the version of the schema language released in 2016, dropped unknown fields while reading in its first releases, 3.0 to 3.4. So every read, change and write by old code quietly erased the new data. Protobuf 3.5.0, released in November 2017, made Java, C++ and Python keep them again. Java can still ask for the old behaviour with DiscardUnknownFieldsParser, and the Try it shows what that costs. Lesson 3 shows the same loss with JSON, where nothing keeps the bytes for you.

Defaults have a catch. In proto3, a plain int64 amount_minor that is 0 isn't written at all. So a reader can't tell "this payment was free" from "this writer has no amount field". Declare it optional int64 amount_minor = 3; when the difference matters. Then the code that Protobuf generates from the .proto file, a Java or Kotlin class per message, gets a method hasAmountMinor() that says whether the field was sent.

The rules for changing a schema follow from the bytes:

  • Never change a field's number. In the bytes, the number is the field.
  • Never reuse the number of a deleted field. Old programs, and old payments in files and databases, still use it. Write reserved 3; and the old name, so that protoc, the tool that reads .proto files and generates code, stops the next person.
  • Change a type only within a group that reads the same bytes. int32, int64, uint32, uint64 (no negative numbers) and bool (true or false) are one group, but an old int32 reader cuts off a value that needs 64 bits.
  • Rename freely: names never reach the bytes. (They do reach Protobuf's JSON form, so there a rename breaks old readers.)

Reusing a number is the quiet one. Delete amount_minor = 3, add int64 fee_minor = 3 a year later, and every old reader shows the fee as the amount. Same bits, new meaning, no error. In the café, that's reprinting box 3 with a new question while old blanks still hang on kitchen walls. Lesson 3 tells the story of a trading firm that lost more than $460 million to the same mistake with a switch in its code.

In the bytes, the number is the field. Never change it, and never reuse it.

Numbered fields let any reader skip what it doesn't know. Next, we'll meet a format that drops the numbers too.

try.title: Keep, drop and misread a field
steps: Open UnknownFieldsDemo.kt. A version 2 writer adds risk_score = 6. A version 1 reader decodes the bytes, changes the amount and writes them back: once with the normal reader, and once with DiscardUnknownFieldsParser, which throws unknown fields away. Then a version 3 writer reuses field number 3 for fee_minor.
Predict the three numbers the demo prints: the risk score after each update, and the amount version 1 reads from version 3's record.

code.title: UnknownFieldsDemo.kt (the middle)
code.html: // a v1 service reads v2's bytes, changes the amount and writes them back val read = DynamicMessage.parseFrom(v1, fromV2) println("v1 sees unknown fields: ${read.unknownFields.asMap().keys}") val updated = read.toBuilder().setField(v1.findFieldByName("amount_minor"), 4500L).build().toByteArray() val back = DynamicMessage.parseFrom(v2, updated) println("after v1's update, v2 reads risk_score = ${back.getField(v2.findFieldByName("risk_score"))}") // the same with a parser that throws unknown fields away (what proto3 did before 3.5.0) val discarding = DiscardUnknownFieldsParser.wrap(DynamicMessage.getDefaultInstance(v1).parserForType) val lossy = discarding.parseFrom(fromV2).toBuilder() .setField(v1.findFieldByName("amount_minor"), 4500L).build().toByteArray()

try.expect:
v2 wrote 44 bytes, ending in 30 57
v1 sees unknown fields: [6]
after v1's update, v2 reads risk_score = 87
with DiscardUnknownFieldsParser, v2 reads risk_score = 0
v3 wrote amount 4000 and fee 150; v1 reads amount_minor = 150

The new field costs two bytes: the key 30 (field 6, varint) and 57 (87). The normal reader keeps it through version 1's update, and the discarding reader loses it. The reused number makes version 1 report the fee as the amount, without any error.

sections.h: Avro drops the numbers too: the writer's schema meets the reader's
sections.html:
Protobuf still spends a key byte on every field. Avro spends none. It's a binary format from the Hadoop project, a set of tools for working through huge piles of data on many machines. It was first released in 2009, and its bytes carry neither names nor numbers. An Avro schema is written in JSON, as a list of fields, each with a name and a type:

{"type": "record", "name": "Authorization", "fields": [
  {"name": "paymentId", "type": "long"},
  {"name": "merchant", "type": "string"},
  {"name": "amountMinor", "type": "long"},
  {"name": "currency", "type": "string"},
  {"name": "tags", "type": {"type": "array", "items": "string"}}
]}

Here is the same payment in Avro, 38 bytes:

a2 80 da 87 e8 e8 d8 a9 33          paymentId: 1849204436731904017 (ZigZag varint)
16 46 65 72 6e 20 42 ...            merchant: length 11 (ZigZag of 11 is 22, 0x16), "Fern Bakery"
c0 3e                               amountMinor: 4000 (ZigZag 8000)
06 45 55 52                         currency: length 3, "EUR"
04 08 63 61 72 64 06 33 64 73 00    tags: 2 items, "card", "3ds", then 0 for the end of the list

The values follow each other in the schema's field order. Every whole number and every length is a varint after ZigZag, the trick from the first section that turns -1 into 1 and 1 into 2. Nothing in the bytes says where merchant starts, or that it's text. So a reader can't even skip a field without knowing its type. It needs the exact schema the writer used. Give it the wrong one and you get nonsense, not an error. In the Try it, reading these bytes with a two-field writer's schema returns amountMinor: 11, which is really the length of "Fern Bakery".

In the café, an Avro order is a sheet with no box numbers at all, only answers in order. You can read it only against the exact blank form it was filled in on.

So a change is handled when the data is read. The reader brings two schemas: the writer's schema, to decode the bytes, and its own reader's schema, the shape its code wants. Avro matches the two by field name:

  • A field in both is decoded. If the types differ, only some widenings are allowed: int to long, float or double; long to float or double; float to double; string to bytes and back. (In Avro, int is a 32-bit whole number, long a 64-bit one, and float and double are numbers with fractions.)
  • A field only in the writer's schema is decoded and thrown away.
  • A field only in the reader's schema gets the reader's default value. With no default, the read fails.

That makes the rule for changing an Avro schema short: add or remove only fields that have a default. A field that may be missing is usually written as ["null", "string"] with "default": null, which means "either nothing or text, and nothing when it's missing". The null must come first for that default to be valid.

Where does a reader find the writer's schema? There are three answers, one for each way data travels:

  • A big file of records keeps the schema once, at the start. An Avro container file begins with Obj and the byte 1, then the schema as JSON, then blocks of records with a 16-byte marker between them. A thousand payments took 38,336 bytes in the Try it.
  • Records stored or sent one at a time carry a short number, a schema ID. A schema registry, a separate program that stores schemas by number, turns the number back into the schema. Kafka is a program that keeps logs of messages for other programs to read. The tools that Confluent, a company built around Kafka, makes for it put a 0 byte and a 4-byte schema ID in front of each record. The Stream processing track's lesson Schemas, Connect and change data capture covers that side.
  • Two programs that talk over one network connection can agree on schemas when the connection opens.

Why go without numbers at all? Because then a program can write the schemas for you. Copy a database table (rows and columns, like a spreadsheet) to Avro, and each column becomes a field. When someone adds a column, the copy has a new writer's schema, and nobody has to hand out field numbers and promise never to reuse them. That's why Avro is common for moving data in bulk between systems. Protobuf is the usual choice for messages that people design by hand. One example is gRPC, a way for one program to call another over the network (lesson 4 of this track).

Either way, a change can still break a reader that someone forgot about. Next, we'll let a program check every change before it ships.

try.title: Read Avro with the right, a newer and the wrong schema
steps: Open AvroDemo.kt. It writes the payment with a GenericRecord, Avro's record that needs no generated class. Then it reads the bytes three times: with a reader's schema that adds a field channel with a default, with one that adds it without a default, and with a wrong writer's schema. Last, it writes 1,000 records to a container file.
Predict which of the three reads fails loudly, and which returns wrong data quietly.

code.title: AvroDemo.kt (the reads)
code.html: // a newer reader adds a field with a default: Avro matches fields by name and fills the gap val readerWithDefault = avro("$V1_FIELDS, {\"name\": \"channel\", \"type\": \"string\", \"default\": \"card\"}") val r = GenericDatumReader<GenericRecord>(writer, readerWithDefault) .read(null, DecoderFactory.get().binaryDecoder(bytes, null)) // decoding with the wrong writer schema: the bytes say nothing about their own layout val wrongWriter = avro("""{"name": "paymentId", "type": "long"}, {"name": "amountMinor", "type": "long"}""") val garbage = GenericDatumReader<GenericRecord>(wrongWriter) .read(null, DecoderFactory.get().binaryDecoder(bytes, null))

Avro: 38 bytes
a2 80 da 87 e8 e8 d8 a9 33 16 46 65 72 6e 20 42 61 6b 65 72 79 c0 3e 06 45 55 52 04 08 63 61 72 64 06 33 64 73 00
reader with channel (default card): {"paymentId": 1849204436731904017, "merchant": "Fern Bakery", "amountMinor": 4000, "currency": "EUR", "tags": ["card", "3ds"], "channel": "card"}
reader with channel, no default: Found sfz.payments.Authorization, expecting sfz.payments.Authorization, missing required field channel

The missing default fails loudly. The wrong writer's schema fails quietly: the reader takes 16, the length of "Fern Bakery", as amountMinor (22 after undoing ZigZag is 11) and stops, with no error. In the container file the schema costs a few hundred bytes once, and each record costs its 38.

aside.title: If the reader needs the writer's schema, why not send it with every record?
aside.html: You could, and each record would then describe itself, like JSON. But the schema is usually far bigger than one record. Our payment's schema is a few hundred bytes of JSON, and the record is 38. Sending it once per file, once per connection, or as a 4-byte number keeps the saving. Avro also has a middle way, called single-object encoding: it puts an 8-byte fingerprint of the schema, a short number worked out from its text, in front of each record.

sections.h: Compatibility has two directions, and a registry checks them before you deploy
sections.html:
Picture the day of a change. The payment program already writes version 2 of the schema, the payout program still reads with version 1, and a year of version 1 records sits in storage. Every reader has to cope with every writer. Here are the two directions once more, because people swap them all the time:

  • Backward compatible: new code can read data written by old code. Updating the readers first is safe.
  • Forward compatible: old code can read data written by new code. Updating the writers first is safe.

A running system needs both. Stored data stays for months, so new readers meet old data. And while a new version replaces the old one machine by machine, old readers meet records from writers that have already changed. Kafka calls a program that writes records a producer, and one that reads them a consumer.

Checking this by eye doesn't hold up for long. Someone forgets that a field has no default, or that old data still holds version 1. A schema registry turns the check into a gate. Each version of a schema is registered under a subject, a name for one stream of records. By default there's one subject per Kafka topic, Kafka's name for one log of messages. Before the registry accepts a new version, it checks it against the older ones. It uses the format's own rules: Avro's matching rules from the last section, or Protobuf's rules for numbers and types. The direction of the check is the subject's compatibility mode. Confluent Schema Registry offers these:

Mode The new schema must Update first
BACKWARD (the default) read data written with the latest version consumers
FORWARD be readable by the latest version producers
FULL do both either side
NONE nothing you're on your own

Each of the first three has a _TRANSITIVE twin, which checks every registered version, not only the latest.

In the café, the registry is the office that checks each new form design against the old ones before it goes to the printer.

The default holds a trap. BACKWARD compares a new version only with the one before it. Take a payment schema whose version 1, v1, has amount as an int. v2 removes amount, and a v2 reader skips it in old data, so v2 passes. v3 brings amount back as a string with a default, and a v3 reader of v2 data uses the default, so v3 passes too. But a v3 reader that meets a v1 record finds an int where it wants a string, and fails. And old records do stay around: in a compacted topic, which keeps the newest record for each key forever, or in a table with five years of rows. Use the _TRANSITIVE modes whenever old data is kept. Confluent recommends BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE for Protobuf. The figure shows the chain, and in the lab your own registry check rejects it.

A mode is also a deploy order. BACKWARD means consumers first; FORWARD means producers first. Teams often update the producer first, because it's their own program. Under BACKWARD, nobody promised the old consumers anything, and they fail on the first new record.

Protobuf teams usually put the gate in the build, the automatic step that compiles and tests code before it ships. Buf, a set of tools for Protobuf, has a command, buf breaking, that compares your .proto files with the last released ones. It fails the build on, for example, a deleted field whose number isn't reserved (FIELD_NO_DELETE_UNLESS_NUMBER_RESERVED) or a changed type (FIELD_SAME_TYPE). Its default setting, FILE, also flags renames, because they break the generated code. The setting WIRE checks only the bytes, and Buf recommends WIRE_JSON as the minimum, which protects the JSON form too.

Here is where a registry stops: it checks shapes, not meaning. Change amount from euros to cents, keep the type long, and every check passes while every old reader is now wrong by a factor of 100. A change like that needs a new field and a migration, a planned move of the old data to the new shape. That's lesson 3.

try.title: Predict the compatibility table
steps: Before you run anything, write down yes or no under BACKWARD, FORWARD and FULL for each change: add a field with a default, add one without, remove a field that had a default, remove one that didn't, widen int to long, rename a field, and rename it with an alias (a second, old name that Avro also accepts).
Run CompatibilityDemo from the labs folder. It asks Avro's SchemaCompatibility check about both directions for each change, then checks the v1, v2, v3 chain from the figure.
For each wrong guess, say which reader fails and why: the new reader on old data (BACKWARD), or the old reader on new data (FORWARD).

code.title: CompatibilityDemo.kt (the check)
code.html: fun canRead(reader: Schema, writer: Schema) = SchemaCompatibility.checkReaderWriterCompatibility(reader, writer).type == COMPATIBLE for ((what, new) in changes) { val backward = canRead(new, old) // new readers, old data val forward = canRead(old, new) // old readers, new data println("%-36s %-9s %-9s %s".format(what, yes(backward), yes(forward), yes(backward && forward))) }

rename amount, no alias              no        no        no
rename amount, with an alias         yes       no        no

v2 reads v1: yes   v3 reads v2: yes   v3 reads v1: no
reader type: STRING not compatible with writer type: INT

Widening works one way only. A new long reader widens old ints, but an old int reader can't take a long. An alias lets the new reader find the old name, while the old reader still has no idea what amountMinor is. Only changes to fields with defaults pass all three.

refs.title: Buf: Breaking change rules and categories

opening:
Picture a café that takes catering orders on a paper form. Every box on the form has a number: box 1 is the name, box 3 the amount, box 5 any notes. The cooks keep a blank copy on the wall and read each order by box number, never by the printed questions.

One week the café adds box 6, for allergies, and prints a new form. The night cook still has last month's blank, which stops at box 5. An order arrives with something written in box 6.

It's easy to think everyone must switch to the new form on the same day. They can't. Old orders sit in drawers for months, and someone always gets the new blank a week late.

In From objects to bytes, field names took more than half of every record. In this lesson, we'll replace the names with numbers, read the bytes one at a time, and watch old code meet a field it has never seen. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a café that added box 6 to its form while the night cook still used last month's. Protobuf's answer is the cook's: read every box by number, keep the unknown ones and pass them on, and never print a new question in an old box. Avro reads each sheet against the exact form it was filled in on.

Next time a chat app shows a message it can't display and asks you to update, notice what it didn't do: crash. An old reader met something new, found where it ended, and skipped it.

Next, we'll run two versions of one program side by side, and ask what happens to stored data while the old one keeps writing.

compare.title: The same payment in Protobuf (42 bytes) and Avro (38 bytes)

a.label: Protobuf
a.title: key, then value, per field
a.html:
08                              key: field 1, varint
91 80 ed 83 b4 b4 ec d4 19      1849204436731904017
12 0b                           key: field 2, LEN; 11 bytes
46 65 72 6e 20 42 61 6b 65 72 79  "Fern Bakery"
18 a0 1f                        field 3: 4000
22 03 45 55 52                  field 4: "EUR"
2a 04 63 61 72 64               field 5: "card"
2a 03 33 64 73                  field 5: "3ds"

compare.note: Protobuf spends one key byte per field, seven here, so that any reader can find the end of each field and skip what it doesn't know, with or without the writer's schema. Avro spends nothing on keys and ends the list with one byte instead. That makes it 4 bytes smaller, but unreadable without the exact writer's schema. Protobuf pays bytes to be independent of the writer; Avro pays with a registry or a schema at the start of the file.

worked.title: Replace a field in a Protobuf message without breaking anyone

steps.say: The fraud team wants string channel = 6, free text such as "card", "Card" or "CARD-PRESENT", replaced by an enum, a type with a fixed list of named values. You can't change the type of field 6: a string and an enum use different wire types, so old readers would treat the value as unknown. So add a new field with a new number, and give the enum a zero value that means "not set".

Writers fill in both fields for as long as any reader may use field 6. New readers prefer field 7, and fall back to field 6 when field 7 is CHANNEL_UNSPECIFIED, which is what they see in every record written before the change.
steps.code: // subgoal: read the new field, fall back to the old one fun channelOf(a: Authorization): Channel = if (a.channelType != Channel.CHANNEL_UNSPECIFIED) a.channelType else when (a.channel.lowercase()) { "card", "card-present" -> Channel.CHANNEL_CARD_PRESENT "web", "ecommerce" -> Channel.CHANNEL_ECOMMERCE else -> Channel.CHANNEL_UNSPECIFIED }

steps.say: When no program reads field 6 any more, and no stored data that matters still depends on it, delete it. Reserve both its number and its name, so nobody can bring back field 6 with a different meaning.

Make the build enforce it. A buf.yaml file with the WIRE_JSON setting checks every change against the main branch, the shared copy of the code. Deleting field 6 without the reserved line, or changing its type, fails buf breaking --against '.git#branch=main' before the change can go in.
steps.code: # buf.yaml (subgoal: the gate runs on every pull request) version: v2 breaking: use: - WIRE_JSON

lab.title: Varints by hand, a Protobuf codec that skips unknown fields, and a registry gate
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 21 fail with NotImplementedError, Kotlin's error for code nobody has written yet. You don't need Docker, the tool other labs use to start databases.

In Varint.kt, write encode, decode and zigzag. VarintTest compares your bytes with what protobuf-java's CodedOutputStream writes for 206 values, including Long.MIN_VALUE, the most negative Long, and -1.

In ProtoCodec.kt, write key, then encode for the five fields. ProtoCodecTest checks your 42 bytes against what protobuf-java writes for the same record, so the order of the fields, and the rule that a zero value isn't written, must match.
Write decode. It must read protobuf-java's bytes, skip the fields 6 and 7 that a version 2 writer adds, and leave default values for fields that aren't there.

In RegistryGate.kt, write canRead with Avro's SchemaCompatibility, then isCompatible for every mode. The last tests replay the v1, v2, v3 chain from the lesson, and decode a real v1 record with a v3 reader.
Run the tests until all 21 pass.
hints: In encode, loop while v ushr 7 != 0L: write (v and 0x7f) or 0x80, then v = v ushr 7. Use ushr, which shifts zeros in from the left, not shr, or a negative number never reaches zero.
In decode, bytes[i].toInt() and 0xff turns a Kotlin Byte, which runs from -128 to 127, into 0 to 255 before you test bit 7.
ZigZag is one line: (n shl 1) xor (n shr 63). Here shr is right: it copies the sign bit into all 64 bits.
In ProtoCodec.decode, split a key with key ushr 3 (the field number) and key and 7 (the wire type). Skip by wire type, never by field number: that's what lets old code read new data.
BACKWARD means canRead(candidate, old), and FORWARD means canRead(old, candidate). The _TRANSITIVE modes check every item of registered, and the others only registered.last().

drill.title: Write varint encode and decode from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson. Write encode(value: Long): ByteArray and decode(bytes: ByteArray, offset: Int): Pair<Long, Int> for Protobuf varints. Check them on paper: 150 must give 96 01, and -1 must take 10 bytes.

answer.html: fun encode(value: Long): ByteArray { val out = ByteArrayOutputStream() var v = value while (v ushr 7 != 0L) { // unsigned shift: -1 takes 10 bytes out.write(((v and 0x7f) or 0x80).toInt()) v = v ushr 7 } out.write(v.toInt()) // last byte: top bit clear return out.toByteArray() } fun decode(bytes: ByteArray, offset: Int): Pair<Long, Int> { var result = 0L var shift = 0 var i = offset while (true) { val b = bytes[i++].toInt() and 0xff result = result or ((b and 0x7f).toLong() shl shift) if (b and 0x80 == 0) return result to i shift += 7 } }

recap: A schema replaces field names with an agreement both sides keep. Protobuf writes a key per field, the field number times 8 plus a wire type, then the value: 42 bytes for the payment, against 116 for JSON.
Varints use 7 bits per byte, lowest bits first: cheap for small numbers, but 10 bytes for a negative int64 unless you declare sint64, which applies ZigZag.

The wire type lets old code skip a field it doesn't know, and keep it (forward compatibility). Missing fields read as defaults (backward compatibility). Never change or reuse a field number: reserve it.
Avro writes only values, so a reader needs the writer's exact schema, which it matches against its own by field name, using defaults. Add or remove only fields that have defaults.

A registry's mode names both the check and the deploy order: BACKWARD means consumers first, FORWARD producers first. Modes without _TRANSITIVE check only the latest version, so use the transitive ones when old data is kept.
The limit: a registry checks shapes, not meaning. A field that changes from euros to cents passes every check, and needs a migration.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why Protobuf needs field numbers that can never be reused, while Avro has no numbers at all. Explain what each format writes, and what each reader needs.
explain.answer: Protobuf writes, for each field, a key made of the field number and a wire type, then the value. The wire type tells any reader how long the value is, so a reader with an older schema can skip a field it doesn't know, and even keep it, without the writer's schema. That only works if a number means the same thing forever. If field 3 was the amount and is later reused for a fee, old readers decode the fee as the amount with no error, so deleted numbers get reserved. Avro writes only the values, in the schema's field order, so the bytes don't describe themselves at all. A reader must have the exact writer's schema, from the file's start or a registry ID, and then Avro matches the writer's fields to the reader's by name, using defaults for missing ones. With no numbers there's nothing to reuse, and a program can write the schemas, for example from database tables. The price is that every reader depends on finding the writer's schema.

deeper.html:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd edition, chapter 5) compares Thrift, Protobuf and Avro, and argues that a schema is documentation that can't go out of date, because decoding needs it. Martin Kleppmann's 2012 post "Schema evolution in Avro, Protocol Buffers and Thrift" has the byte-by-byte comparison that chapter grew from.

Editions. Newer .proto files replace the syntax = "proto3" line with a line like edition = "2024" (from protoc v32, released in 2025). Editions turn the old differences between proto3 and proto2, the version before it, into settings you can choose per file or per field, such as field_presence. The bytes don't change, so old data stays readable. Edition 2026 is still being written.

Thrift. Apache Thrift, from Facebook, follows Protobuf's design: numbered fields and a type in the bytes. Its CompactProtocol comes within a byte or two of Protobuf's size, and its older BinaryProtocol is much bigger.

ASN.1. Protobuf and Thrift reinvent ideas from ASN.1 (1984), whose DER encoding still carries every X.509 certificate, the files that prove a website's identity (the Computer networking track's lesson on TLS). It also evolves with tag numbers, and its complexity is a warning about schema languages that try to do everything.

Zero-copy formats. FlatBuffers and Cap'n Proto keep numbered fields like Protobuf, but lay them out so a reader can use a field where it sits, without decoding the whole message. Apache Arrow's IPC format does the same for whole columns.

Schema IDs in headers. Since Confluent Platform 8.1.1, a serializer can put the schema's ID in a Kafka header, a small labelled value that travels beside a record, instead of the 5-byte prefix. Deserializers check the header first and fall back to the prefix, so a fleet of programs can switch over while it's being updated. The Stream processing track picks this up.
